Congenital CNS Disorders
LO 1–6 Spastic ~75–80% Non-progressive lesion

🧠 Cerebral Palsy

🎯 How Boards Would Word It

"A 2-year-old boy, born at 27 weeks' gestation, is brought in because he is not yet walking independently. Exam shows increased tone and hyperreflexia in both lower extremities, a scissoring gait when held upright, and a positive Babinski sign. MRI of the brain shows loss of periventricular white matter. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?"

The stem almost always anchors cerebral palsy to a prematurity/perinatal-injury history plus the stereotyped triad — abnormal tone, a recognizable movement pattern (spastic / dyskinetic / ataxic), and delayed motor milestones — with imaging showing an old, non-progressing lesion (periventricular leukomalacia if preterm, parasagittal watershed injury if term). Any answer choice implying a progressive course is a trap; that's what rules CP out.

▶
▶ Cerebral palsy (CP) — causes, symptoms, diagnosis, treatment, pathology
Video — "Cerebral palsy (CP) — causes, symptoms, diagnosis, treatment, pathology" (YouTube)
LO 1 · Natural History

Epidemiology & Etiology

The most common cause of chronic childhood motor disability. Reported incidence runs roughly 2–3.6 per 1,000 live births (figure varies slightly by source), with U.S. prevalence around 1 million people.

Most cases are idiopathic — there's no single identifiable cause in the majority of children. When a risk factor is identifiable, the two biggest are preterm birth and low birth weight, which are also the most heavily tested. Other contributors:

  • Perinatal hypoxic-ischemic injury / birth asphyxia
  • Intracranial hemorrhage, periventricular leukomalacia
  • Chorioamnionitis / maternal-fetal infection, TORCH infection
  • Structural brain malformation
  • Kernicterus (untreated severe hyperbilirubinemia)
  • Postnatal CNS infection (meningitis, encephalitis)
  • Multiple gestation, antepartum bleeding, prolonged second stage of labor
  • Maternal thyroid disorder in pregnancy

Defining feature: the causative insult happens before the cerebrum finishes developing — in utero through roughly the first 2–3 years of life — and the resulting lesion itself is static/non-progressive. The clinical picture can still evolve as the child grows (contractures, scoliosis, worsening function) even though the underlying brain injury isn't getting worse — that distinction is a common exam trap.

Pathophysiology — Timing Determines the Lesion Pattern

Hypoxic-ischemic insult
→
Timing of injury
→
Lesion location
→
Clinical subtype

Preterm brain

  • Periventricular leukomalacia — ischemic white-matter loss near the lateral ventricles (a watershed zone at this gestational stage)
  • Corticospinal fibers to the legs run closest to the ventricles → spastic diplegia is the classic result

Term brain

  • Parasagittal (watershed) injury — cortical border-zone loss along the ACA–MCA–PCA boundaries
  • Broader cortical involvement → mixed/spastic quadriplegia; deep gray/basal ganglia injury (e.g., kernicterus, severe asphyxia) → dyskinetic (athetoid) patterns
Cerebral palsy subtypes — spastic (diplegia / hemiplegia / quadriplegia) vs. non-spastic (dyskinetic, ataxic) — click to zoom
LO 2 · Clinical Presentation

General Pattern

CP is rarely diagnosed at birth — it usually surfaces once a child starts missing motor milestones (not rolling over, not sitting independently by the expected age). Diagnosis is clinical. Comorbidities span all subtypes: seizure disorder (~35–50%), intellectual disability (~50–67%), vision/hearing impairment, behavioral difficulty/ADHD.

Spastic (~75–80%)

  • ↑ tone, ↑ DTRs, persistent primitive reflexes (positive Babinski)
  • Toe-walking / equinus deformity
  • Scissoring gait (hip adductor spasticity)
  • Muscle weakness/atrophy, hip dislocation, scoliosis risk
  • Subtypes: diplegia (legs > arms — classic preterm pattern), hemiplegia (one side), quadriplegia (all four limbs, most severe, most tied to seizures/intellectual disability)

Non-spastic (dyskinetic / ataxic, >20%)

  • Involuntary movements that worsen with stress, resolve in sleep
  • Chorea, athetosis, dystonia (dyskinetic)
  • Intention tremor, poor coordination, wide-based gait (ataxic)
  • Dysarthria and dysphagia common

⚠ Red Flag

A definite hand preference before age 1 is abnormal — normal infants aren't lateralized that early. It suggests weakness of the unused hand and should raise concern for hemiplegic CP on the side opposite the preferred hand.

LO 3 · Diagnostic Workup
StudyWhy it's done / what it shows
Clinical assessment (H&P + standardized motor/developmental tools)Primary basis for diagnosis — confirms the tone/movement pattern and helps exclude a progressive disorder
Cranial ultrasound (neonatal period)Screens preterm infants (open fontanelle) for intraventricular hemorrhage, periventricular leukomalacia, or gross structural anomaly
MRI brain (preferred, especially older infants)Most sensitive study — identifies periventricular leukomalacia, parasagittal watershed injury, cortical malformation, or old hemorrhage
EEGReserved for infants with suspected seizures, not part of routine diagnostic workup
Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI)Newer modality mapping white-matter tract integrity; increasingly used in advanced/research workup

Differential to Exclude

Because CP is defined by a static lesion, a progressive course on follow-up should prompt work-up for: hypothyroid myopathy, mitochondrial myopathy, progressive muscular dystrophy, myelomeningocele, traumatic peripheral nerve injury, or an underlying genetic syndrome. (List not exhaustive.)

LO 4 · Treatment

Multidisciplinary — No Cure, Goal Is Function

Non-pharmacological

  • Physical therapy — prevents/manages contractures
  • Occupational therapy — motor skill / ADL training
  • Speech therapy — communication, dysphagia
  • Orthotic & assistive devices (braces, splints, walkers, wheelchairs)
  • Nutritional support for dysphagia
  • Educational, social & psychological support
  • Adjunctive: myofascial/soft-tissue OMM for secondary musculoskeletal strain from chronic spasticity (not standard-of-care per AMBOSS/course materials, but a reasonable structural adjunct)

Pharmacological

  • Antispasmodics — botulinum toxin (focal), baclofen, dantrolene, benzodiazepines
  • Anticonvulsants if seizures present
  • Anticholinergics for rigidity / sialorrhea

Surgical

  • Orthopedic surgery — scoliosis correction, contracture release
  • Selective dorsal rhizotomy — relieves spasticity and pain
LO 5 · Monitoring & Long-Term Complications

What to Track

  • Hip surveillance — periodic imaging for subluxation/dislocation from chronic adductor tone imbalance, especially in higher-tone motor types
  • Feeding/aspiration risk from dysphagia → growth and nutrition monitoring
  • Bone health — osteopenia/osteoporosis risk (reduced weight-bearing ± antiepileptic effects)
  • Chronic musculoskeletal pain from contractures and abnormal biomechanics
  • Adult survivors carry increased long-term risk of cardiovascular disease, cerebrovascular disease, and digestive disorders — a good reminder that CP isn't only a pediatric diagnosis
LO 6 · Prevention & Health Promotion

Modifiable Levers

  • Antenatal magnesium sulfate given to birthing parents at risk of imminent preterm delivery (e.g., expected to deliver within 24 hours) has a neuroprotective effect on the fetus and is associated with a reduced incidence of cerebral palsy
  • Treating maternal thyroid disease during pregnancy
  • Minimizing delivery complications; prompt recognition/management of birth asphyxia
  • General preterm-birth prevention strategies — though because most cases remain idiopathic, prevention has real limits

💡 Pearl

Antenatal MgSO₄ is one of the few interventions with real evidence for lowering CP incidence — that's usually the "prevention" answer choice on LO6-style questions, so don't confuse it with its other big use case (seizure prophylaxis in preeclampsia/eclampsia).

🧠 Practice Questions — Cerebral Palsy
LO 1–3 Type I most common ♀ > ♂

🔻 Chiari Malformation

🎯 How Boards Would Word It

"A 17-year-old girl presents with several months of occipital headaches that worsen with coughing, straining, and exertion, along with new unsteadiness and double vision. Neurologic exam shows dysarthria, gait ataxia, and a pattern of nystagmus where the eyes drift slowly upward and then jerk sharply downward. MRI of the brain shows the cerebellar tonsils extending several millimeters below the foramen magnum. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?"

The stem almost always pairs a Valsalva-provoked occipital headache with cerebellar signs (ataxia, dysarthria, downbeat nystagmus) in an adolescent or young adult — that's the Type I pattern, and "downbeat nystagmus" is a near-pathognomonic buzzword for it. Swap the patient to a newborn with a myelomeningocele plus obstructive hydrocephalus, stridor, and feeding trouble, and the answer flips to Type II instead.

▶
▶ Chiari Malformation | Type I and II Chiari Malformation
Video — "Chiari Malformation and Treatment | Type I and II Chiari malformation" (YouTube)
LO 1 · Natural History

Epidemiology & Associations

Type I is the most common Chiari subtype overall. Reported figures vary by source — roughly 1 in 1,000 in the general population, with MRI-based prevalence around 0.6% in adults and 0.9% in children; more common in females.

Type II (Arnold-Chiari malformation) is the most common serious malformation of the posterior fossa, and is essentially always accompanied by myelomeningocele and hydrocephalus.

Associations across the group: neural tube defects (especially meningomyelocele), syringomyelia, hydrocephalus, Klippel-Feil syndrome, and basilar invagination.

Definition & Pathophysiology

Chiari malformations are dysraphisms — defects in embryonic midline closure — affecting structures related to the metencephalon/posterior fossa, resulting in caudal displacement of the cerebellar tonsils (± vermis, ± medulla) through the foramen magnum.

Primary causes: genetic factors (retinoic acid receptor–FGF signaling), failure of neural tube or surrounding mesenchymal closure, an undersized posterior cranial fossa, possible nutritional contribution.
Secondary/acquired: trauma, tumor or cyst, excessive CSF drainage (e.g., an over-draining shunt).

Several competing mechanistic theories are proposed:

  • Fluid theory — a neural tube defect causes CSF leakage → reduced posterior fossa volume → cerebellar/tonsillar compression and downward displacement
  • Molecular genetic theory — a primary congenital defect of posterior brain and bony structures
  • Growth abnormality theory — poorly coordinated cranial and cervical bone growth
  • Crowding theory — an undersized posterior fossa crowds neural tissue at the foramen magnum
Posterior fossa underdevelopment / dysraphism
→
Crowding at foramen magnum
→
Caudal herniation of cerebellar tissue
→
CSF flow disruption
→
Syrinx / hydrocephalus
Normal vs. Chiari types I–III — click to zoom

Type I

  • Ectopic extension of the cerebellar tonsils through the foramen magnum only
  • Strongly associated with syringomyelia (~90% of idiopathic syrinx cases have a Type I lesion)
  • Not typically associated with hydrocephalus in children (<10%), though it can cause adult-onset hydrocephalus
  • Associated with occipital dysplasia

Type II (Arnold-Chiari)

  • Downward displacement of cerebellar tonsils, vermis, and medulla oblongata (± 4th ventricle)
  • Small posterior fossa; bony/dural abnormalities; tectal plate deformation
  • Almost always accompanied by hydrocephalus and myelomeningocele

Type III

  • Herniation of cerebellar and brainstem tissue through an abnormal posterior skull opening (occipital/cervical encephalocele)
  • Most severe subtype; 4th ventricle enlargement, occipital lobe herniation
LO 2 · Clinical Presentation

General Pattern

Type I is typically asymptomatic in infancy and childhood; symptoms, when they appear, usually emerge around puberty or early adulthood. Type II is virtually always symptomatic in infancy, given its essentially universal association with myelomeningocele.

Type I CM

  • Occipital headache, classically worsened by Valsalva (coughing, straining) and physical activity
  • Neck pain; radicular pain in the shoulders/arms
  • Lower cranial nerve dysfunction
  • Cerebellar signs: dysarthria, ataxia
  • Downbeat nystagmus (pathologic slow upward drift + fast downward corrective saccade)
  • May develop syringomyelia and/or (less often) hydrocephalus over time — up to 14% of pediatric Chiari I in one series had a documented syrinx
  • In children: progressive cerebellar ataxia, lower-extremity spasticity, scoliosis, weakness; rare apneic episodes in infants
  • Usually not associated with hydrocephalus

Type II CM (Arnold-Chiari)

  • Usually symptomatic in infancy
  • Obstructive hydrocephalus from aqueductal compression by displaced tissue
  • Breathing difficulties/apneic episodes, feeding difficulties
  • Lower cranial nerve findings: laryngeal stridor, tongue fasciculations, sternocleidomastoid paralysis, deafness, bilateral abducens (CN VI) palsy
  • Always accompanied by myelomeningocele → motor/sensory deficits at and below the lesion level
  • May also develop syringomyelia

Type III: mostly fatal in early infancy. Survivors can have upper and lower motor neuron palsies, cranial nerve dysfunction, cerebellar signs, epilepsy, and intellectual disability.

⚠ Distinguishing Red Flags

Valsalva-provoked occipital headache + cerebellar signs in a teen/young adult → think Type I. Obstructive hydrocephalus + myelomeningocele + lower cranial nerve findings in an infant → think Type II.

LO 3 · Diagnostic Workup
StudyFindings
Lateral radiographs of head/neckHistorically used to suggest a craniocervical junction anomaly; largely superseded by MRI
CT brainCan show a small posterior fossa and hydrocephalus; less sensitive than MRI for tonsillar position and soft-tissue detail
MRI brain, T2-weighted sagittal (± axial) — preferred, most sensitiveType I: low-lying cerebellar tonsils extending below the foramen magnum, small posterior fossa, ± syrinx, usually no hydrocephalus.
Type II: additional caudal displacement of the vermis, medulla, and 4th ventricle; tectal beaking; often accompanied by hydrocephalus.
Type III: cerebellum/medulla herniating through an osseous defect in the occipital/cervical skull (encephalocele)

💡 Pearl

Type I is defined by isolated tonsillar herniation — no vermis, no myelomeningocele, usually no hydrocephalus. The moment a question adds vermis/4th-ventricle displacement plus hydrocephalus plus myelomeningocele, you're looking at Type II, not Type I.

🧠 Practice Questions — Chiari Malformation
LO 1–3 Most common posterior fossa malformation ~1 : 25,000–35,000 births

🫧 Dandy-Walker Malformation

🎯 How Boards Would Word It

"A newborn is noted to have an unusually large head circumference and a soft, fluctuant bulge over the back of the skull. Brain MRI shows an enlarged posterior cranial fossa, complete absence of the cerebellar vermis, and a large cystic structure occupying the space normally filled by the fourth ventricle. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?"

The classic triad is (1) cerebellar vermis agenesis/hypoplasia, (2) cystic dilation of the 4th ventricle (a persistent Blake's pouch), and (3) an enlarged posterior fossa — usually with obstructive (noncommunicating) hydrocephalus riding along. Any stem combining macrocephaly + a posterior fossa cyst + an absent vermis is pointing at Dandy-Walker, not garden-variety hydrocephalus.

LO 1 · Natural History

Epidemiology

  • The most common posterior cranial fossa malformation
  • Incidence roughly 1 per 25,000–35,000 live births
  • Accounts for approximately 1–4% of hydrocephalus cases

Definition, Etiology & Pathogenesis

A dysraphism of the metencephalon — failure of the fourth ventricle's roof to close normally leads to persistence of Blake's pouch (a fetal 4th-ventricle outpouching) as a cystic dilation, together with agenesis/hypoplasia of the cerebellar vermis and an enlarged posterior cranial fossa. Brainstem dysplasia can accompany the picture.

Proposed contributors include genetic disorders and environmental insults, with reported associations to congenital rubella infection and fetal alcohol syndrome.

Pathology clue: the enlarged posterior fossa pushes the confluence of sinuses above the level of the lambdoid suture because of an abnormally high-riding tentorium — a finding termed torcular-lambdoid inversion.

4th ventricle roof fails to close
→
Persistent Blake's pouch / cystic 4th ventricle
→
Vermis agenesis + enlarged posterior fossa
→
Obstructed CSF outflow
→
Noncommunicating hydrocephalus
LO 2 · Clinical Presentation

Presentation

  • Early newborn signs: macrocephaly (enlarged head circumference) and a bulge or lump at the back of the skull
  • Developmental delay — walking, talking
  • Vision and hearing impairment
  • Seizures; abnormal eye movements
  • Ataxic gait and poor coordination/balance — driven by the absent/hypoplastic vermis
  • Neurologic abnormalities are compounded by the accompanying noncommunicating hydrocephalus

Associated Extracranial Anomalies

Screen for other congenital anomalies at diagnosis — Dandy-Walker malformation is associated with craniofacial abnormalities, cardiac defects, and spina bifida.

LO 3 · Diagnostic Workup
StudyFindings
MRI brain (preferred) or CTEnlarged posterior fossa; absent/hypoplastic cerebellar vermis; cystic dilation of the 4th ventricle (persistent Blake's pouch); torcular-lambdoid inversion (high tentorium, confluence of sinuses above the lambdoid suture); ± noncommunicating hydrocephalus; ± corpus callosum hypoplasia
MRI T2 sagittal — cystic/hyperintense posterior fossa, hypoplastic cerebellum, enlarged posterior fossa. Click to zoom
MRI T2 sagittal, age 4 — vermis hypoplasia, cystic 4th ventricle, high tentorium, callosal hypoplasia. Adapted from Krupa & Bekiesińska-Figatowska, BioMed Research International (Hindawi, open access) — click to zoom

Differential — Other Causes of Noncommunicating Hydrocephalus

Worth distinguishing on imaging before settling on Dandy-Walker: intrauterine infection (e.g., congenital toxoplasmosis/TORCH), a colloid cyst obstructing the interventricular foramen, and congenital aqueductal stenosis — none of which reproduce the vermis-agenesis + cystic-4th-ventricle + enlarged-fossa triad.

💡 Pearl

Torcular-lambdoid inversion — the venous confluence sitting above the lambdoid suture from a high-riding tentorium — is a distinctive imaging clue for Dandy-Walker beyond just "big cystic 4th ventricle," and a nice differentiator from a simple arachnoid cyst or mega-cisterna magna.

🕳️ Spina Bifida

⚠ Source material caps this disease at LO 1, 2 & 6 specifically — Diagnostic Workup, Treatment, and Monitoring are intentionally not built here even though some diagnostic content exists in the source, per the stratification given.

🎯 How Boards Would Word It

"A newborn is noted to have a large, thin-walled cystic sac protruding from the lower back at the thoracolumbar junction, with visible neural tissue and nerve roots within the sac. Maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein had been elevated at 16 weeks' gestation. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?"

Board stems for open spina bifida (myelomeningocele/myeloschisis) almost always pair an elevated maternal serum/amniotic AFP with a visible midline cystic mass containing neural elements. Contrast that with spina bifida occulta, which is a closed defect — often an incidental finding (skin dimple, hair tuft) with a completely normal AFP — that's the detail that separates the two on a question stem.

LO 1 · Natural History

Epidemiology & Terminology

Spina bifida is a neural tube defect (NTD) — the most common category of congenital CNS abnormality. Synonyms: spinal dysraphism, open neural tube defect (for the open subtypes).

  • NTD incidence has been declining; a recent New England estimate places it around 0.77 per 1,000 births
  • Spina bifida occulta is the most common NTD subtype overall
  • ~75% of myelomeningoceles occur in the lumbar region

Pathophysiology & Etiology

Fundamental mechanism: the neural tube fails to seal along the midline (or reopens after initially closing), leaving the posterior vertebral arch unfused, with variable involvement of the meninges and neural elements depending on severity.

Risk factors — genetic, nutritional, and environmental:

  • Folic acid deficiency (the single most modifiable factor)
  • Family history (~5% of cases)
  • Anticonvulsant medications
  • Pre-existing maternal diabetes and obesity
  • High maternal fevers in early pregnancy
Normal vs. spina bifida occulta, meningocele, myelomeningocele — click to zoom

Spina bifida occulta

  • Midline vertebral arch defect only
  • No involvement of the meninges or neural components
  • Closed defect — skin remains intact over it

Meningocele

  • Vertebral arch defect + herniation of the meninges only
  • Neural structures remain in the canal
  • Open defect

Myelomeningocele

  • Vertebral arch defect + herniation of meninges and neural tissue
  • Most severe of the three classic subtypes
  • Open defect

Broader classification spectrum (for recognition): closed forms also include lipomyelomeningocele and lipomeningocele (fat tissue included, covered by skin); open forms also include myeloschisis/rachischisis (the most severe subtype — neural tissue completely fails to fuse and is left bare, with no meningeal, bony, or skin coverage) and myelocele (spinal cord herniates without meningeal coverage).

LO 2 · Clinical Presentation

By Subtype

  • Spina bifida occulta: generally asymptomatic — often an incidental finding. Subtle overlying skin changes may be present at the level of the defect (dimple, hair tuft, fatty subcutaneous mass, discoloration)
  • Meningocele: a fluid-filled, cyst-like sac extends off the back at the level of the dysraphism; typically no neurologic deficits, since neural tissue isn't involved
  • Myelomeningocele: a cystic structure covered by a thin, often incompletely epithelialized membrane with visible/palpable neural tissue. Causes deficits determined by lesion level — lumbar myelomeningoceles (the most common location) typically cause lower-extremity paralysis and loss of bladder/bowel control. Often accompanied by hydrocephalus, associated skeletal anomalies (clubfoot, sacral dimpling, joint contractures), and developmental delay
Open spina bifida — cystic structure herniating at the thoracolumbar junction. Click to zoom
Lumbar region, neonate — protruding cystic lesion with hypertrichosis. © IMPP — click to zoom
Close-up of the protruding lesion — exposed/raw neural tissue visible. © IMPP — click to zoom

⚠ Distinguishing Clue

A hair tuft, skin dimple, or fatty subcutaneous mass overlying the lumbosacral spine in an otherwise well-appearing infant should prompt screening for an occult (closed) spinal dysraphism — the infant can look outwardly normal.

LO 6 · Prevention & Health Promotion

Modifiable Prevention

  • Folic acid supplementation during pregnancy is the single most effective preventive measure — recommended for all people of childbearing potential, with higher doses for those with a prior NTD-affected pregnancy or other risk factors (e.g., taking an antiepileptic medication)
  • Optimizing glycemic control in pre-existing diabetes
  • Weight management
  • Using the lowest effective dose of known teratogenic anticonvulsants where possible
  • Avoiding hyperthermia (e.g., high fevers, hot tubs) in early pregnancy

💡 Pearl

Folic acid supplementation is one of the highest-yield "prevention" answer choices on OB/peds-flavored boards questions — reflexively reach for it whenever a stem mentions neural tube defects and prevention in the same breath.

🧠 Practice Questions — Spina Bifida
LO 1–5 Noncommunicating ~70% / Communicating ~30% 0.5–0.8 / 1,000 births

💧 Pediatric Hydrocephalus

🎯 How Boards Would Word It

"A 2-month-old boy is brought in for a routine well-child visit. His head circumference has crossed from the 50th to the 97th percentile since birth. Exam shows a tense, bulging anterior fontanelle, prominent scalp veins, and downward deviation of both eyes with visible sclera above the iris. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?"

Accelerating head growth crossing percentiles, plus a bulging fontanelle and the "sunset sign" (downward eye deviation), is the signature infant hydrocephalus triad — the open sutures let the skull expand to buffer rising pressure before the classic adult-style signs show up. Swap in an older child with closed sutures and the same underlying process instead looks like garden-variety raised ICP: headache, vomiting, and papilledema.

LO 1 · Natural History

Epidemiology & Risk Factors

Pediatric hydrocephalus is not itself a disease — it's a finding (excess CSF in the ventricular/subarachnoid compartments) with a shared clinical picture regardless of the underlying cause. Incidence runs roughly 0.5–0.8 per 1,000 births (live or stillborn).

Risk factors: low birth weight, prematurity, maternal diabetes, low socioeconomic status, male sex, familial aggregation (1st/2nd-degree relatives); incidence is lower in Asian populations.

Etiology & Pathophysiology

Acquired (most common trigger overall): intraventricular/intracerebral hemorrhage — typically prematurity-related — plus tumor and infection.
Congenital: roughly half of congenital cases involve 4th-ventricle abnormalities — Chiari malformation, Dandy-Walker malformation — plus neural tube defects and aqueductal stenosis.

CSF overproduction or outflow obstruction
→
CSF accumulates proximal to the problem
→
Ventricular enlargement ± ↑ICP

Communicating (~30%)

  • No obstruction — all ventricles and the subarachnoid space enlarge together
  • ↑ CSF production — choroid plexus tumor/hyperplasia
  • ↓ CSF absorption — congenital deficiency of arachnoid granulations, or scarring of granulations after meningitis/hemorrhage

Noncommunicating (~70%)

  • Obstruction somewhere in the ventricular system (aqueduct of Sylvius, foramen of Luschka/Magendie) — only the ventricles upstream of the blockage enlarge
  • Classic infant causes: Chiari malformation, Dandy-Walker malformation, aqueductal stenosis; tumor in older children

Evolving classification: a newer proposed schema would reserve the term "communicating" only for choroid-plexus overproduction, reclassifying everything else — including classic absorption-defect cases — as "obstructive," since CSF flow is blocked somewhere along the ventricular or subarachnoid pathway either way. Worth recognizing both schemes.

LO 2 · Clinical Presentation

Presentation Changes With Suture Status

  • Infant (open sutures): abnormal or accelerated head growth crossing percentiles, macrocephaly, tense/bulging fontanelle, prominent scalp veins, sunset sign (downward eye deviation, sclera visible above the iris — from pressure on the tectal/vertical-gaze region), positive Babinski sign, brisk reflexes, spasticity, clonus, irritability, poor feeding, developmental delay
  • Young child (sutures fusing): brisk reflexes, spasticity, clonus — head growth less dramatic as compensation weakens
  • Older child (closed sutures): presentation is more subtle to spot early since the skull can no longer expand — irritability, lethargy, poor appetite, vomiting, headache, personality change, plus long-tract signs

Once compensation fails at any age: headache, nausea/vomiting, papilledema, abnormal gait, impaired consciousness, abducens (CN VI) palsy, and — as a late, decompensated finding — Cushing triad (irregular respirations, widening pulse pressure, bradycardia).

MacEwen ("cracked pot") sign: percussing the skull near the frontal-temporal-parietal junction produces an unusually resonant sound from separated sutures — seen in late hydrocephalus.

Manifestations of ↑ICP in infants — click to zoom
Sunset sign — both eyes deviated downward. Click to zoom
LO 3 · Diagnostic Testing
StudyUse
History & physical examHead circumference trend/percentile crossing, fontanelle tension, tone/reflex exam
Cranial ultrasoundPreferred initial study in infants with an open anterior fontanelle (< 18 months)
MRI brain (preferred) or CT headUsed once the fontanelle closes (≥ 18 months) and in older children; identifies the ventricular pattern and often the causative lesion
Evans ratio (on imaging)Ratio of frontal horn width to biparietal diameter; > 30% supports ventriculomegaly
Lumbar punctureOnly after a mass lesion is excluded — measures opening pressure and allows CSF sampling; used selectively, not first-line in obstructive disease

Differential — Hydrocephalus Ex Vacuo

A common imaging mimicker: the ventricles and subarachnoid space look enlarged from loss of brain tissue (e.g., prior injury, atrophy) rather than CSF accumulation. ICP and CSF flow are normal, and it's asymptomatic from a hydrocephalus standpoint — worth excluding, especially in a child with a history of significant brain injury.

LO 4 · Treatment

Temporizing vs. Definitive

Medical / temporizing

  • Reduces CSF production for interim relief: acetazolamide, furosemide (diuretics)
  • Serial lumbar punctures or external drainage in select acute settings

Surgical / definitive

  • Extracranial shunting — most commonly a ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt (inflow catheter, reservoir, valve, outflow catheter)
  • Endoscopic third ventriculostomy (ETV) — alternative in select obstructive cases
  • Cerebral aqueductoplasty — reopens a stenotic aqueduct of Sylvius

Shunt Complications

  • Infection — most commonly gram-positive organisms (e.g., Staphylococcus epidermidis) — typically requires shunt removal
  • Mechanical obstruction
  • Underdrainage → recurrent elevated ICP; overdrainage → intracranial hypotension, and chronic overdrainage can cause slit ventricle syndrome (ventricular collapse + shunt obstruction)
LO 5 · Monitoring & Complications

Long-Term Follow-Up

Outcome depends heavily on the underlying etiology. Ongoing complications to track:

  • Developmental delay
  • Memory problems
  • Visual problems
  • Behavioral issues

Surveillance includes serial head-circumference growth curves, developmental screening, and ongoing monitoring for shunt malfunction — shunt complications can present at any point after placement, not just early on.

💡 Pearl

In infants, hydrocephalus "hides" behind an open fontanelle — the skull expands to buffer rising ICP, so the overt late signs (papilledema, Cushing triad) show up late. Once the sutures fuse, that same pressure has nowhere to go, and the picture shifts to look like classic adult-pattern raised ICP.

🔍 Related Entity — Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus (Adults)

Don't confuse this infant-focused picture with NPH — a distinct, adult-onset (> 60 years) form of chronic communicating hydrocephalus with normal or only mildly elevated ICP. Classic triad, the "3 Ws": Wet (urinary incontinence), Wacky (dementia), Wobbly (gait apraxia). Diagnosed with MRI (ventriculomegaly out of proportion to sulcal atrophy) plus a CSF tap test — gait improving after removing 30–50 mL of CSF supports the diagnosis. Same underlying "hydrocephalus" name, completely different patient and presentation.

LO 1–4 Sagittal suture most common ~1 : 2,000–2,500 births

🧩 Craniosynostosis

🎯 How Boards Would Word It

"A 4-month-old boy is brought in because his parents noticed his head appears unusually long and narrow from front to back, with a palpable ridge along the midline of the scalp. His skull is narrow in the transverse plane but elongated anteroposteriorly. Which of the following sutures is most likely fused prematurely?"

The stem almost always anchors craniosynostosis to a specific head-shape word tied to the fused suture — a long, narrow, "boat-shaped" skull (scaphocephaly) points to the sagittal suture, the most commonly affected. Swap the shape descriptor and the answer changes: triangular forehead → metopic (trigonocephaly); short/broad/flat → bilateral coronal (brachycephaly); twisted/oblique face → unilateral coronal or lambdoid (plagiocephaly). And don't confuse any of these with positional plagiocephaly, a soft-tissue molding issue with patent sutures — not true craniosynostosis.

LO 1 · Natural History

Epidemiology & Risk Factors

Primary (isolated) craniosynostosis occurs in roughly 1 in 2,000–2,500 live births (estimates vary by source).

Potential risk factors: positive family history, advanced maternal age, nicotine use during pregnancy, and use of clomiphene citrate for infertility treatment.

Etiology & Pathophysiology

Cranial membranes form by month 2 of development; the cranial bones form from these membranes by month 5. Rapid brain growth subsequently shapes the cranial bones through open sutures and fontanelles, which allow both compression during birth and ongoing skull expansion as the brain grows.

The cause of isolated (nonsyndromic) synostosis is unknown but is thought to reflect disrupted, unbalanced growth forces. At the molecular level, mutations affecting fibroblast growth factor (FGF), FGF receptor, and/or TGF-β signaling between the dura mater and the suture mesenchyme lead to premature fusion — this same pathway underlies syndromic craniosynostosis (occurring as part of a genetic syndrome).

Premature suture fusion
→
Growth restricted perpendicular to that suture
→
Compensatory growth along remaining open sutures
→
Characteristic skull shape
Normal sutures vs. sagittal craniosynostosis (scaphocephaly) vs. metopic craniosynostosis (trigonocephaly) — click to zoom
LO 2 · Clinical Presentation

General Pattern

Most infants are otherwise asymptomatic — craniosynostosis is usually recognized purely from an abnormal head shape within the first year of life, present at birth and either symmetric or asymmetric depending on which suture(s) are involved. If more than one suture is affected, the child may develop signs of increased ICP and/or hydrocephalus from restricted cranial growth.

Suture(s) InvolvedResulting ShapeFeatures
Sagittal — most common overall (reported ~45–80% depending on source); more common in malesScaphocephaly / dolichocephalyLong, narrow, "boat-shaped" skull
Unilateral coronal — 2nd most common; more common in females, often syndrome-associatedAnterior (frontal) plagiocephalyLaterally twisted/oblique skull and face; shallow orbit and face rotated toward the affected side
Bilateral coronalBrachycephaly (or oxycephaly/turricephaly if untreated)Short A-P skull, widened transversely, tall forehead; if untreated, an abnormally tall "tower" skull can develop
Unilateral lambdoid — rare, M:F ≈ 4:1Posterior (occipital) plagiocephalyTwisted/oblique skull, occipitoparietal flattening and a low-set ear on the affected side (~70% right-sided, can be bilateral)
Metopic — < 10–25% of cases depending on source; associated with 19p chromosome abnormalityTrigonocephalyTriangular-shaped forehead, prominent occiput/parietal eminences, hypotelorism (close-set eyes)
Multiple sutures (esp. metopic + coronal + lambdoid) — rare, most severeCloverleaf (trilobar) skullProminent forehead with temporal bulging; often associated with hydrocephalus and elevated ICP

⚠ Not the Same Thing — Positional Plagiocephaly

Positional plagiocephaly — a flattened or oblique head shape from external positioning (e.g., consistently sleeping on one side) — is frequently mistaken for craniosynostosis but is a completely separate, benign entity with a different mechanism. Unlike true craniosynostosis, it does not restrict skull growth, and imaging shows patent (open) sutures. Infant torticollis is another mimicker that also shows patent sutures on imaging.

LO 3 · Diagnostic Testing
StudyFindings / Role
Inspection & palpationPrimary method — craniosynostosis is mainly a clinical diagnosis based on head shape and a palpable ridge along the fused suture
Skull X-ray (AP + lateral)Bony bridging across the suture, or loss of normal suture lucency
Cranial CT with 3D reconstructionAssesses the extent of fusion, identifies coexisting hydrocephalus, and helps plan surgical reconstruction — reserved for cases needing further workup, not obtained routinely
LO 4 · Treatment

Surgical Is the Mainstay

Surgical (definitive)

  • Indicated in essentially all confirmed cases — to prevent/treat cerebral constriction (elevated ICP) and for cosmetic correction
  • Techniques: strip craniectomy, cranial vault remodeling
  • Timing is somewhat controversial; most commonly performed around 3–9 months of age

Nonsurgical

  • Manipulation/repositioning has a limited role in true craniosynostosis
  • It's far more relevant to the positional plagiocephaly mimicker, which — unlike true suture fusion — can improve with repositioning or helmet therapy

💡 Pearl

Match the shape word to the suture: scaphocephaly = sagittal, trigonocephaly = metopic, brachycephaly = bilateral coronal, plagiocephaly = unilateral coronal (anterior) or lambdoid (posterior), cloverleaf skull = multiple sutures with hydrocephalus. And always screen out positional plagiocephaly (patent sutures) before calling it true craniosynostosis.

🍷 Sturge-Weber Syndrome

⚠ Source material caps this disease at LO 1 & 2 — Diagnostic Workup, Treatment, and Monitoring are intentionally not built here, even though the NIH source covers them, per the stratification given.

🎯 How Boards Would Word It

"A 6-month-old girl has had a port-wine-colored birthmark involving the skin above her right eye and forehead since birth. At 13 months, she develops recurrent focal clonic seizures affecting the left side of her body. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?"

Board stems pair a facial port-wine stain in the ophthalmic (V1) trigeminal distribution with seizures that begin after the first year of life and are contralateral to the birthmark — that laterality detail is the classic testable link, since the leptomeningeal vascular malformation sits under the same side as the skin lesion, and it's that affected hemisphere generating seizures on the opposite side of the body.

LO 1 · Natural History

Epidemiology & Classification

Sturge-Weber syndrome (SWS) is a rare neurocutaneous disorder — this category of conditions is also known as the phakomatoses. Synonyms: encephalotrigeminal angiomatosis, SWS.

Incidence is approximately 1 in 20,000 live births.

Etiology & Pathophysiology

Caused by a random, non-inherited mutation in the GNAQ gene — found in ~88% of patients with SWS. The mutation presents as somatic mosaicism: only a subset of a person's cells carry the variant, which is why blood vessels form abnormally in some regions but not others.

GNAQ mutation → aberrant Gq signaling in endothelial cells → decreased blood flow through leptomeningeal capillaries → chronic cortical hypoxia.

Pathology: the overlying leptomeninges become overvascularized (the vascular malformation itself), while the underlying brain parenchyma is undervascularized and develops calcifications and atrophy from chronic hypoxia. Significant calcifications around the gyri are often visible on imaging. Thrombosis of cortical veins can occur in the affected region.

GNAQ somatic mosaic mutation
→
Aberrant Gq signaling in endothelial cells
→
Leptomeningeal capillary malformation
→
Chronic cortical hypoxia
→
Cortical calcification + atrophy
Sturge-Weber syndrome — mechanism, port-wine stain distribution, and associated CNS/ocular findings. Click to zoom
LO 2 · Clinical Presentation

Cutaneous

Facial nevus (port-wine stain): present at birth in most patients, involving the skin around the eye/forehead along the ophthalmic (V1) division of the trigeminal nerve. Color ranges from light pink to deep purple, reflecting a high density of dermal capillaries.

Neurologic

  • Glaucoma and buphthalmos (enlarged eyeball from elevated intraocular pressure) may develop in the ipsilateral eye — can cause blindness if untreated
  • Seizures typically develop after the first year of life — focal, clonic, and contralateral to the facial nevus; may worsen with age
  • Transient stroke-like episodes or visual deficits from cortical vein thrombosis in the affected region — can cause unilateral weakness or memory/cognitive changes

Psychiatric / Developmental

  • Developmental delay and learning problems typically emerge only after the first year of life
  • Intellectual disability and severe learning disabilities occur in roughly 50% of cases
  • Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder

⚠ High-Yield Laterality Link

Seizures are contralateral to the facial birthmark — the leptomeningeal vascular malformation sits on the same side as the skin lesion, and it's that affected cortex generating seizure activity on the opposite side of the body.

💡 Pearl

The single biggest prognostic clue in SWS: seizure onset before age 2 that is resistant to treatment predicts a much higher risk of intellectual disability. Timing and treatment response — not just the presence of the birthmark itself — is what drives long-term outcome.
